name: crewAI

facts.description: Framework for orchestrating role-playing, autonomous AI agents. By fostering collaborative intelligence, CrewAI empowers agents to work together seamlessly, tackling complex tasks.

title: crewAI: A Python Framework for Orchestrating Autonomous AI Agents
answer: crewAI is an open source Python framework, made by CrewAI Inc and released under the MIT licence, for orchestrating role playing autonomous AI agents that collaborate on complex tasks. It sits above the model layer, letting you define agents with roles, goals and backstories, assign them tasks and tools, and run them as a crew. The one thing to know before adopting it is that its production story pairs flexible agent reasoning with Flows, a deterministic backbone for control, cost and auditability.

sections.body: crewAI is an open source framework for building and orchestrating multi agent AI workflows, maintained by CrewAI Inc and distributed under the MIT licence, with its code at github.com/crewAIInc/crewAI and its home at crewai.com. The site describes it as a framework for orchestrating role playing, autonomous AI agents, where collaborative intelligence lets agents work together on complex tasks. It is written in Python, and the repository shows a last push on 2 October 2026. In the AI stack it sits above the model layer: it does not train or serve models itself, it coordinates agents that are powered by language models, so it belongs to the orchestration and application layer rather than to model development or inference infrastructure.
sections.heading: What it is and where it sits in AI work

sections.body: The framework is used for multi step work that benefits from several specialised agents rather than one prompt. On the site, an agent is an autonomous entity defined by a role, a goal and a backstory, which can use tools and is powered by a language model, while a task is a unit of work assigned to an agent and a crew is a collection of agents and tasks run under a process such as sequential execution. A worked tutorial shows a researcher agent with a web search tool producing a report on emerging technologies, and the site lists role based crews with specialists such as researcher, analyst and writer, shared memory and handoffs. It is strongest where tasks need reasoning over unstructured data, tool and API calls, and collaboration between agents, such as research, analysis, drafting and review, and the site positions it for production automations with tracing, guardrails and an Agent Management Platform. It is not presented as a training framework or as a model serving system.
sections.heading: What it is used for and where it is strongest

sections.body: The official material suggests a moderate learning curve for a working Python developer. The tutorial installs the crewai and crewai-tools packages, sets an API key in a .env file, and then defines agents, tasks and a crew in ordinary Python, with concepts such as role, goal, backstory, task, process and kickoff introduced as they are used. No mathematics or systems prerequisites are stated on the pages read, and the site does not present a formal beginner course or curriculum. What it does offer a newcomer is a developer portal, a quick tutorial with complete code in a GitHub repository, and agent ready documentation including an MCP server and an llms-full.txt file, which are aimed at developers who already know Python and have access to a language model API.
sections.heading: How hard it is to learn and what you need first

sections.body: The site shows an ecosystem built around model providers, tools and enterprise platforms. A tutorial integrates Cerebras inference, running Llama 3.1 8B and 70B on the Wafer Scale Engine 3, and installs crewai-tools alongside the core package. An announcement describes a collaboration with NVIDIA to integrate crewAI with NVIDIA NIM microservices, part of NVIDIA AI Enterprise, so that models hosted on NVIDIA can power agents and flows, with a demo using Meta's Llama 3.3 and a blueprint on NVIDIA. The framework is compared on the site with Microsoft Agent Framework, AutoGen, MetaGPT and Automation Anywhere, and the site lists documentation, a developer portal, an MCP server and an Agent Management Platform. The repository facts record 59,291 stars, and a blog page cites 40,000 GitHub stars at the time of the NVIDIA announcement, alongside 1.4 billion agentic automations and 60 percent of the Fortune 500.
sections.heading: Ecosystem and community

sections.body: The site presents crewAI as serving both ends, but with a deliberate split. Crews of role based agents give quick, flexible prototypes, and the same crews and flows are said to ship from prototype to production with tracing, guardrails and enterprise governance. For production, the site's guidance article argues that the gap in agentic AI is architecture rather than intelligence, and describes Agentic Systems that combine Flows, a deterministic backbone, with intelligence deployed where it matters. Flows are described as a very thin code layer with almost no abstractions, using decorators and state management, handling conditional branching, state across steps and custom business logic, with the same inputs following the same execution path, event driven and modifiable at runtime. The cost of that control is that some behaviour must be expressed as explicit flow logic rather than left to agent autonomy, and the site itself criticises both heavy scaffolding that cannot adapt and unbounded agency without constraints.
sections.heading: Prototyping speed against production performance

sections.body: The material read supports adoption claims but not a full market picture. The site says crewAI is used in production at large enterprises such as PwC and startups such as Parloa, that it has processed agentic workflows for companies in healthcare, consumer packaged goods, finance, logistics and professional services, and that DocuSign cut sales research time from hours to minutes using its architecture. A CrewAI survey report, based on 500 C level executives and senior leaders at organisations with over 100 million dollars in revenue, reports that 65 percent of organisations already use AI agents, 81 percent have fully adopted or are actively scaling agentic AI, and 57 percent prefer building on existing open source tools rather than starting from scratch. The site does not state whether crewAI is a de facto standard or a legacy choice, and it gives no salary or hiring data, so a reader choosing it for work should treat those questions as unsettled by the official material.
sections.heading: Industry adoption and careers

sections.body: crewAI is Python first, and the site frames it as the open, Python first option for multi agent crews, in contrast with Microsoft Agent Framework, which targets .NET and Azure ecosystems and is recommended when standardising on Azure AI services, and Automation Anywhere, an enterprise RPA platform with AI assisted bots for UI and legacy system automation. The site notes that many enterprises use RPA for deterministic UI workflows and crewAI for cognitive, language heavy automations, which is the polyglot pattern it belongs to: a Python orchestration layer calling language models, tools and APIs, sitting alongside existing automation and cloud stacks rather than replacing them. Its model layer is provider agnostic in the examples shown, with Cerebras and NVIDIA hosted models both demonstrated, so it is typically used with whichever inference provider a team already has.
sections.heading: How it fits beside the others

sections.body: The official pages are candid about some weaknesses and silent on others. The guidance article says most implementations are either too rigid or too loose, criticises prompt chains passing as agents, graph based designs on maintainability grounds, and autonomous agents without architectural constraints, which implies that naive use of the framework alone is not enough for production. The token spend article says extended reasoning can consume tens of thousands of tokens before a short answer, that a ten step run can reach 500,000 to two million tokens, and that a large share of enterprise token spend goes to use cases that have not proven business value. The site does not state benchmark performance, latency or memory characteristics, does not give a formal comparison of agent quality against other frameworks, and does not say how the framework handles very large scale concurrency. The survey figures come from CrewAI itself, so they should be read as vendor published rather than independent.
sections.heading: Limits and open questions
